title: Knowing When to Move to GPU
blurb: Tests the fixed cost of PCIe transfers, why pinned memory helped less than expected, arithmetic intensity and why elementwise work never wins on the GPU, the matmul crossover, the roofline view, and the checklist for deciding to offload.

refLinks.label: §55.2.1 Transfer Overhead Is Real, and Textbook Mitigations Aren’t Guaranteed
§55.2.2 A Memory-Bound Operation: GPU Never Wins
§55.2.3 A Compute-Bound Operation: A Real, Computable Crossover
§55.2.4 The Roofline Model: Why These Two Cases Diverge

questions.prompt: Why is moving data to the GPU slow compared with either side's own memory?
options: The GPU must decompress every array it receives from the host.
PCIe is a much narrower pipe than either side's own memory bus.
GPU memory is slower than CPU memory for writes of any size.
The CPU copies the data twice for each transfer, once per direction.
questions.explanation: The interconnect, not either processor's memory, limits transfers. The round trip implied about 3.9 GB/s at the largest size.

refLinks.label: §55.2.1 Transfer Overhead Is Real, and Textbook Mitigations Aren’t Guaranteed

questions.prompt: A 1,000-element round trip took 0.025 ms, implying 0.32 GB/s. Why so low?
options: Small transfers are routed through the CPU's L1 cache first.
The GPU was asleep and had to wake up for this one call.
PCIe slows down when it detects small packets on the bus.
Fixed per-call overhead swamps such a tiny transfer.
questions.explanation: Driver calls and DMA setup cost about the same whatever the size. It is the same shape as Chapter 54's read() overhead.

questions.prompt: Pageable host-to-device took 29.79 ms and pinned 27.65 ms. What is pinned memory's speedup? Give two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 29.79 / 27.65 = 1.077, about 1.08x. Real, but far below the 2–3x sometimes quoted. Measure on your own stack.

questions.prompt: x * 2.0 + 1.0 in float32 does 2 FLOPs per element and moves 8 bytes (one read, one write). What is its arithmetic intensity in FLOPs/byte?
questions.explanation: 2 / 8 = 0.25, and it stays 0.25 at any n, since compute and data grow together.

refLinks.label: §55.2.2 A Memory-Bound Operation: GPU Never Wins

questions.prompt: Using Listing 55.1, matmul intensity is 2n³ / (3n² × 4) = n / 6. What is it at n = 2,048? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 2048 / 6 = 341.3 FLOPs/byte. At n = 64 it is 10.7, and at 4,096 it is 682.7. It grows linearly with n.

options: Counting the output array in the bytes moved
Judging GPU-worthiness by the data size alone
Computing intensity before running any benchmark at all
Using float32 instead of float64 for the estimate
questions.explanation: A 100-million-element elementwise op still lost on the GPU. The ratio of compute to data decides it, and that ratio can stay flat however large the array.

questions.prompt: Why can't a bigger array make x * 2.0 + 1.0 worth offloading?
options: The GPU runs elementwise operations on its slower CUDA cores only.
Its intensity is fixed, so the transfer cost always dominates.
Bigger arrays don't fit in GPU memory on the reference rig.
PyTorch turns large elementwise ops into Python loops.
questions.explanation: Doubling n doubles both compute and bytes. There is no size at which compute outgrows the transfer cost.

refLinks.label: §55.2.2 A Memory-Bound Operation: GPU Never Wins

questions.prompt: What was the GPU's best result on the elementwise op, including transfers?
options: 10x once the arrays were pinned in host memory
1.5x at every size above one million elements
0.98x at n = 100,000, a near-tie and never a win
3.2x at n = 100,000,000, the largest size tested
questions.explanation: Everything else was 0.3–0.6x, including 0.39x at 100 million. The GPU never won across six orders of magnitude.

questions.prompt: Where did matmul cross over to favour the GPU, including transfers?
options: It never crossed over, like the elementwise case
Only at n = 4,096, the largest size tested
At n = 512, after losing at 256
At n = 64, the smallest size tested
questions.explanation: 0.77x at 256, then 1.08x at 512, peaking at 3.21x at 2,048 and settling at 2.52x at 4,096.

questions.prompt: In roofline terms, why does matmul eventually win on the GPU?
options: It doesn't need to transfer its inputs at all.
It moves fewer bytes than elementwise operations of the same size.
Its intensity climbs past the ridge into compute-bound territory.
It runs entirely in the GPU's L2 cache, which avoids PCIe.
questions.explanation: Below the ridge, bandwidth caps performance. Above it, peak compute does, and the GPU's peak compute far exceeds the CPU's.

refLinks.label: §55.2.4 The Roofline Model: Why These Two Cases Diverge

questions.prompt: The matmul speedup rose to 3.21x at n = 2,048 and fell to 2.52x at 4,096. How does the chapter read that?
options: The crossover reversed, so 4,096 belongs on the CPU after all.
Intensity falls at large n, which slows the GPU down.
The 4,096 result was a measurement error and should be ignored.
Measurements wobble. The GPU still clearly wins past the crossover.
questions.explanation: Intensity keeps rising with n. The dip is ordinary measurement shape, and 2.52x is still a substantial win.

refLinks.label: §55.2.3 A Compute-Bound Operation: A Real, Computable Crossover

questions.prompt: What does Procedure 55.2's benchmark include that a naive GPU benchmark often leaves out?
options: The time to start the Python interpreter for the job
The full round trip, with synchronize calls before and after
The compile time of the PyTorch kernels used by the operation
The cost of writing the result to disk afterwards
questions.explanation: Compute-only timing overstates the gain. CUDA is asynchronous, so missing synchronize calls under-reports GPU time.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 55.2 say never to borrow a crossover point from another machine?
options: The crossover is random and changes on every single run.
It depends on the GPU, PyTorch version and PCIe generation.
Crossover points are secret and vary by vendor licence.
Each machine has a different matmul formula for its FLOPs.
questions.explanation: Transfer speed and compute throughput both differ across stacks. Measure the crossover where the work will run.

questions.prompt: Which steps are on Procedure 55.3's checklist? Select all that apply.
options: Move every operation over a million elements to the GPU
Apply the CPU-side levers from Chapters 48–54 first
Measure the crossover on the target hardware
Check whether arithmetic intensity grows with problem size
questions.explanation: The fourth step is reusing data on the GPU across operations before copying back. A size cut-off is exactly the size-only judgement the chapter warns against.

questions.prompt: Why does reusing data across several GPU operations change the decision?
options: The GPU compiles reused operations into one kernel automatically.
One transfer cost is then spread across many operations.
Reuse lowers each operation's arithmetic intensity.
Reused data stays in the CPU cache, which avoids PCIe.
questions.explanation: It is the same amortisation lesson as Chapter 41's resident SAXPY and Chapter 53's pool reuse.

questions.prompt: A pipeline normalises 50 million floats (elementwise), then runs a 4,096 × 4,096 matmul on them, then copies the result back. Which plan fits the chapter?
options: Transfer once, keep both steps on the GPU, and measure it there.
Keep everything on the CPU, since the elementwise step never wins on a GPU.
Offload only the elementwise step, since it touches the most data.
Copy the data to the GPU and back separately for each of the two steps.
questions.explanation: The matmul's high intensity justifies the transfer. Once the data is on the GPU, doing the cheap elementwise step there avoids a second round trip. Separate round trips per step waste the transfer.

bookExercises.prompt: Define arithmetic intensity in one sentence, and state which of this chapter's two measured operations has an intensity that grows with problem size.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Arithmetic intensity is the number of FLOPs performed per byte of data moved. Of this chapter's two measured operations, matmul's intensity grows with problem size (roughly $O(n)$), while the elementwise operation's stays constant (~0.25 FLOPs/byte) regardless of $n$.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain why the elementwise operation `x * 2.0 + 1.0` never becomes worth moving to GPU, no matter how large `n` gets, using this chapter's roofline framing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The elementwise operation's arithmetic intensity (~0.25 FLOPs/byte) never grows no matter how large $n$ gets. It stays fixed by the operation's structure (2 FLOPs and 8 bytes moved per element). Since it never crosses the ridge point separating memory-bound from compute-bound, the fixed transfer overhead is never amortised away by more compute, so it never becomes worth the GPU round-trip at any size.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 55.1, compute the arithmetic intensity of a matrix-vector product (`n×n` matrix times a length-`n` vector: `2n²` FLOPs, roughly `n²` float32 elements moved) and state whether it grows with `n` the way matmul's does.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Matrix-vector: $2n^2$ FLOPs over $\sim n^2 \times 4$ bytes moved gives intensity $\approx 2n^2 / (4n^2) = 0.5$ FLOPs/byte, constant, independent of $n$. Unlike matmul (whose intensity grows as $O(n)$ because FLOPs grow as $n^3$ but bytes moved only as $n^2$), matrix-vector's FLOPs and bytes-moved both grow as $n^2$, so their ratio never changes with $n$. It behaves like the elementwise operation, not like matmul, and is unlikely to ever cross the ridge point either.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter measured a matmul crossover between n=256 and n=512. Using Listing 55.2 as a base, describe how you would locate the crossover to within a single power of two on a different GPU, and what you would need to hold fixed for the comparison to be fair.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: To locate the crossover on different hardware: sweep matrix sizes by powers of two (or finer) around the expected crossover region, measuring CPU time and full GPU time (including transfer) at each size with proper warm-up and repeated timing (Chapter 48's discipline) and `torch.cuda.synchronize()` around GPU timing. Hold fixed: data type (float32 vs. float64 changes both compute and transfer cost), whether pinned memory is used, and background system load. The crossover point is specific to the exact CPU/GPU/PCIe/dtype combination being tested, not a universal number.

bookExercises.prompt: A pipeline transfers a 50,000-element array to GPU, runs `x * 2.0 + 1.0`, and transfers it back, once per second, forever. Using this chapter's measured numbers, estimate whether batching ten such calls into one before transferring would help, and why.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The elementwise op never wins at any tested size in this chapter's own results (GPU speedup ranges 0.11x-0.98x, never exceeding 1.0x). Batching ten calls into one transfer would amortise the fixed transfer overhead across more actual compute, likely pushing the GPU closer to breakeven or slightly past it, since the operation is dominated by transfer overhead rather than compute at any single-call size tested. Whether batching alone is enough to cross 1.0x depends on the batched array's resulting intensity, but it's a more promising lever than leaving the calls unbatched.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague wants to move a small "glue" reduction step (summing a 10,000-element array once per pipeline iteration) to GPU because "the rest of the pipeline is already on GPU." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two-sentence case for checking arithmetic intensity before agreeing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "A 10,000-element sum has an arithmetic intensity that doesn't grow with data being 'already on GPU.' Check whether this specific reduction crosses the ridge point on its own merits before moving it, since a low-intensity glue step can still lose to the CPU (or to staying resident on GPU without an extra host round-trip) purely from its own transfer/compute ratio, independent of what the rest of the pipeline does."

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter reports pinned memory giving only a 1.08x improvement, against a commonly quoted 2-3x. Propose one hardware or software factor specific to this book's reference rig that might explain the gap, and state what you'd need to test to confirm it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. One plausible factor: PCIe generation/lane configuration or motherboard chipset specifics on this particular reference rig could cap achievable pinned-memory bandwidth gains below the commonly-quoted figures, which are often measured on different (e.g. server-class, more PCIe lanes) hardware. To confirm, one would need to benchmark the same pinned-vs-pageable comparison across multiple different host/GPU/PCIe configurations and see whether the 1.08x figure is specific to this rig or holds more broadly.

bookExercises.prompt: Skim the abstract and introduction of Williams, Waterman, and Patterson's roofline paper. Identify one claim in the paper's original framing that this chapter's two-operation comparison directly illustrates, and one aspect of the full roofline model (such as multiple ceilings for different optimization levels) that this chapter did not exercise.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. The roofline paper's original claim that achievable performance is capped by either memory bandwidth or peak compute depending on arithmetic intensity is directly illustrated by this chapter's two operations landing on opposite sides of that cap. An aspect the two-operation comparison doesn't exercise is the paper's fuller model of multiple ceilings for different optimization levels (e.g. with/without SIMD, with/without cache blocking). This chapter treats each operation as a single point rather than sweeping across optimization levels the way the full roofline model does.
